text: This is the lock most developers never hear about, but it's quietly protecting every UPDATE statement you write: the update lock.
An UPDATE has to do two things on the same row: find it, by evaluating the WHERE clause — that's a read — and then change it — that's a write. Two operations, back to back.

Here's the trap that creates. If that find-the-row read used a plain shared lock, and two sessions ran an UPDATE against the exact same row at the same instant, both could grab a shared lock — shared locks are mutually compatible, after all — and then both try to upgrade to exclusive to perform the write. Each one waits for the other's shared lock to clear first. Neither ever does. That's a deadlock, caused purely by the locking strategy.

The update lock exists specifically to close that trap. It's compatible with a shared lock, so plain SELECTs can still read the row. But it is NOT compatible with another update lock, and not compatible with an exclusive lock. That one rule means only one session at a time can be in the about-to-maybe-update phase for a given row.

Once SQL Server is actually ready to write, the update lock converts to an exclusive lock, which then behaves exactly like last lesson's X lock — held until commit or rollback. You can catch this transition in sys.dm_tran_locks: request_mode shows U briefly, then flips to X.

So two concurrent UPDATEs against the same row never deadlock against each other in normal use — the second one simply waits its turn. Next up: intent locks, which let SQL Server check for conflicts at a coarse level instead of inspecting every single row.
